title: Feasibility of a minimum retesting interval rule for HbA1c in six primary care practices
subtitle: Four-month pilot with progression criteria before a network-wide rollout
statement: About 18 percent of primary care HbA1c requests arrive less than 80 days after the previous result, when a repeat adds little information and can prompt treatment changes within analytical variation. A laboratory rule that holds early requests, explains why and allows override is ready in the test system. It is not known how often the rule would fire in these practices, how often and why clinicians would override it, whether overrides would be fast enough, whether any hold would delay an important decision, or whether practices would accept it.
whoAffected: Adults with diabetes in 64 practices, the clinicians and practice pharmacists who request HbA1c, phlebotomy and laboratory staff, and the primary care network that must approve the rule.
whatHurts: Early repeats cost patients extra blood draws and time, use reagent and staff time, and can lead to treatment changes based on noise. A badly designed hold could delay testing in pregnancy or after a treatment change.
currentPractice: All HbA1c requests are run whatever the interval; no comment explains retesting intervals.
whyNow: The rule is configured, the reagent contract decision is due in mid 2027, and the network committee wants safety evidence before agreeing.
patientCenteredGoal: People with diabetes have HbA1c measured when the result can change their care, and never have a needed test delayed.
summary: Problem framed as a feasibility question for an interval rule, with safety and acceptability as the decisive uncertainties.
